Lav: This zone has been mapped as a low-hazard quick clay area. Quick clay is present but the risk of a major slide is small in current conditions.
Middels: This zone is classified as medium hazard. Quick clay is present and a slide could be triggered by changes in groundwater, slope cuts, or heavy loads.
Hoey: This zone is classified as high hazard for quick clay slides. Avoid grading, drainage changes, or heavy construction without a geotechnical assessment.
Saerlig hoy: This area has the highest radon awareness class. Indoor radon over the action level is much more likely than average. Measure radon and add mitigation if elevated.
Hoy: At least 20%% of dwellings exceed the 200 Bq/m³ action level. Measure indoor radon, especially in lower floors and bedrooms.
Moderat til lav: Radon concentrations are usually below the action level. A measurement is still the only way to confirm levels in your home.
Usikker: NGU has too little data to classify this area. Treat as unknown and consider measuring.

Solid blue polygons mark NVE flood awareness areas (Flom_aktsomhetsomraade). NVE has identified these as places where flooding could occur. There is no severity grading from the source data — every polygon is shown the same.

Three sub-layers are stacked. Solid color = mapped quick-clay zone with hazard degree (Lav / Middels / Hoey). Striped patterns = areas NVE has investigated; a striped polygon labelled "Omraade uten fare" was checked and found safe.

Four classes from NGU. Purple = Saerlig hoy aktsomhet (highest concern). Red = Hoy aktsomhet (>=20%% of dwellings exceed the 200 Bq/m^3 threshold). Yellow = Moderat til lav. Grey = Usikker (insufficient data). The map cannot predict radon in a specific building — measure the building.

NVE jord/flomskred awareness areas. Polygons mark terrain where soil or debris flows are physically possible based on slope and soil. Not a measured forecast — a "could happen" zone, not a "will happen" one.
NVE wind resource raster — average wind speed at 50 m above ground. Color scale increases with wind strength. Used as a long-term wind potential indicator, not a current weather snapshot.

Install a backflow valve on your drainage to prevent sewage from entering the house.
Raise the threshold to the basement and crawl space.

Check your insurance coverage for flood damage.
Keep gutters and downspouts clear of debris.

Contact a geotechnical engineer if you notice ground movement or cracks in walls.
Avoid altering slopes or removing vegetation near the home without assessment.

Inspect roof tiles and gutters annually for damage.
